questions.scenario: Ledgerline, a 25-developer fintech, uses Claude Code on its payments monorepo. Policy says a human must approve the approach before any file under `billing/` changes, so the team committed `"permissions": { "defaultMode": "plan" }` in `.claude/settings.json`. Most developers see `⏸ plan mode on` and edits stay blocked until they approve a plan. One senior developer, who launches every session on his Windows laptop with `claude --allow-dangerously-skip-permissions` so he can switch to bypass later, reports that during planning Claude edited `billing/rates.ts` and ran a migration script without any prompt. The transcript confirms the session stayed in plan mode the whole time. The team wants to keep plan mode as the default and cannot add CI checks before next week's audit. Which change addresses the root cause?
options: Add a line to the project CLAUDE.md, marked IMPORTANT, stating that Claude must never edit files while it is still in plan mode.
Stop launching with `--allow-dangerously-skip-permissions`: in interactive sessions with bypass available, plan mode's blocks aren't enforced.
Move `defaultMode: plan` into his `~/.claude/settings.json`, because user settings are read after the project file and win on his machine.
Have him prefix risky prompts with `/plan`, which enforces the planning block per prompt even when bypass permissions are available.
questions.why_correct: La doc es explícita: en una sesión interactiva de terminal con bypass disponible, Claude Code NO aplica los bloqueos de plan mode. A Claude se le sigue diciendo que planifique sin editar, pero si intenta un edit o un comando, corre sin prompt. El flag `--allow-dangerously-skip-permissions` es justamente lo que deja el bypass disponible. Sacándolo, plan mode vuelve a bloquear los edits hasta que alguien aprueba el plan.

why_wrong.0: `CLAUDE.md` es guidance: Claude ya estaba instruido a planificar sin editar y aun así editó. El problema es que el harness no está bloqueando, y eso no se arregla con texto.
why_wrong.2: Invierte la precedencia (los settings de proyecto están por encima de los de usuario) y además no ataca la causa: el modo ya era `plan`; lo que rompe el bloqueo es tener bypass disponible.
why_wrong.3: `/plan` entra al mismo plan mode. Con bypass disponible en una terminal interactiva, sus bloqueos tampoco se aplican.

questions.rule: Plan mode bloquea edits, salvo en una terminal interactiva con bypass disponible: si necesitás la garantía, no habilites bypass.
questions.source_quote: In interactive terminal sessions with bypass permissions available, Claude Code also doesn't enforce plan mode's blocks.

questions.scenario: A game studio keeps its 1.2-million-line engine in Perforce, not git. A tools engineer wants Claude Code to migrate 240 independent shader-loader files to a new API. Requirements: a lead must approve how the work is split before anything changes, each unit must be implemented and tested in isolation, and every unit's outcome must be reported separately. On her Windows workstation she runs `/batch migrate every shader loader to the v3 API` from the workspace root, and the command fails because the folder is not a git repository. Converting the depot to git is not an option this quarter. What is the most effective way to keep the `/batch` workflow?
options: Run plan mode once over the whole depot, approve the plan, then switch to `acceptEdits` and let the same session apply all 240 changes.
Write a PowerShell loop that calls `claude -p` once per file with `--permission-mode dontAsk` and a per-file prompt, then review the logs.
Start the session with `claude -w shaders` so Claude Code creates a worktree first, then run `/batch` again from inside that worktree.
Configure a `WorktreeCreate` hook that creates the isolated workspaces from Perforce, which `/batch` accepts in place of a git repository.
questions.why_correct: `/batch` investiga el código, descompone el trabajo en 5 a 30 unidades independientes y presenta un plan. Cuando lo aprobás, lanza un subagente en background por unidad, cada uno en su worktree aislado, y cada uno reporta o abre su PR. Cumple las tres exigencias. La doc dice que requiere un repo git **o un hook `WorktreeCreate`** que cree los worktrees: para un VCS que no es git, ese hook es la vía documentada.

why_wrong.0: Cumple la aprobación previa, pero no la aislación por unidad ni el reporte separado: termina siendo un diff gigante en una sola sesión.
why_wrong.1: Aísla por archivo, pero nadie aprueba la descomposición antes de empezar. Son 240 corridas sueltas sin un plan revisado.
why_wrong.2: `claude -w` arranca la sesión en un worktree nuevo de git. En un workspace Perforce no resuelve nada: sin el hook `WorktreeCreate` sigue sin haber de dónde crear worktrees.

questions.rule: `/batch` = plan aprobado + un subagente por unidad en su propio worktree. Sin git, hace falta un hook `WorktreeCreate`.
questions.source_quote: Requires a git repository or a WorktreeCreate hook that creates the worktrees.

questions.scenario: At an insurance company, the claims-engine repo must start every Claude Code session in plan mode, so the team committed `"defaultMode": "plan"` under `permissions` in `.claude/settings.json`. Developers who use Claude Code in Windows Terminal start in plan mode as expected. The 14 developers who work in the VS Code extension still see new conversations start in Auto; most of them picked Auto from the mode indicator weeks ago. A platform engineer proposes copying the same `defaultMode` into each developer's `~/.claude/settings.json` as the fix. Which change makes new VS Code conversations start in plan mode for those developers?
options: Set `claudeCode.initialPermissionMode` to `plan` in each developer's VS Code user settings, since the extension checks it before anything else.
Copy `defaultMode: plan` into each `~/.claude/settings.json`; the extension falls back to user settings when it ignores the project file.
Move `defaultMode: plan` into `.claude/settings.local.json`, which has higher precedence than the shared project settings file.
Ask developers to pick Plan once from the mode indicator, so the extension remembers it for every new conversation in that folder.
questions.why_correct: La extensión de VS Code nunca lee `.claude/settings.json` ni `.claude/settings.local.json` del proyecto para el modo inicial. Su orden es: 1) `claudeCode.initialPermissionMode`; 2) el último modo elegido en el indicador, si fue Manual, Edit automatically o Auto; 3) `defaultMode` de managed settings o de `~/.claude/settings.json`; 4) el default built-in. Como ya eligieron Auto en el indicador, solo el ítem 1 le gana.

why_wrong.1: Casi: la extensión sí lee `~/.claude/settings.json` (ítem 3), pero el Auto que eligieron en el indicador (ítem 2) está antes en la lista. Siguen arrancando en Auto.
why_wrong.2: La extensión tampoco lee `.claude/settings.local.json` para el modo inicial: el problema no es de precedencia entre archivos del proyecto.
why_wrong.3: Elegir Plan en el indicador aplica solo a esa conversación. La extensión recuerda Manual, Edit automatically o Auto, pero no Plan.

questions.rule: VS Code no lee los settings del proyecto para el modo inicial: `claudeCode.initialPermissionMode` manda.
questions.source_quote: The extension never reads a project's .claude/settings.json or .claude/settings.local.json for the starting permission mode.

questions.scenario: A logistics company asked Claude Code to replace the retry logic in a legacy dispatch module that nobody on the current team wrote: about 35 files, three message queues, and implicit ordering assumptions. Over two days a developer tried three times in auto mode with the prompt `replace the custom retry loop with the shared backoff library`. Each attempt ran about 40 minutes, touched 20+ files, broke ordering guarantees in the integration tests, and was reverted. Token spend for the three attempts was roughly four times a normal feature. The team lead wants the next attempt to fail cheaply if the direction is wrong, and to sign off on the approach before any code changes. What should the developer do first?
options: Raise the session to `/effort max` so Claude verifies more edge cases before editing, then run the same prompt one more time.
Switch to `acceptEdits` and add `run the integration tests after every file` to the prompt, so failures show up much earlier.
Start in plan mode so Claude explores the module and proposes an approach, then approve or redirect it before any edit happens.
Split the task across three parallel subagents, one per queue, so each attempt carries less context and finishes sooner.
questions.why_correct: Es una tarea compleja, en código desconocido y con la dirección en duda: el caso de plan mode. Claude explora y propone un enfoque para que lo apruebes, y eso evita el retrabajo caro cuando la dirección inicial está mal. Cumple las dos restricciones: si el enfoque está mal, se ve en el plan (barato), y el lead firma antes de que se toque el código.

why_wrong.0: Más esfuerzo no te da la aprobación humana previa, y la dirección se sigue descubriendo editando. La doc además avisa que `max` en tareas comunes tiende a sobrepensar.
why_wrong.1: Detecta antes las roturas, pero sigue editando sin que nadie haya aprobado el enfoque: trata el síntoma, no la causa.
why_wrong.3: Paralelizar no arregla una dirección mal elegida. Además las tres colas comparten supuestos de orden, y nadie aprueba nada antes de los edits.

questions.rule: Tarea grande, código desconocido, dirección incierta → plan mode primero. Ejecución directa cuando ya sabés exactamente qué hacer.
questions.source_quote: Claude explores the codebase and proposes an approach for your approval, preventing expensive re-work when the initial direction is wrong.

questions.scenario: A health-tech team needs per-tenant rate limiting on its public API, but the requirements were never written down. A developer spent a three-hour Claude Code session brainstorming: per-user versus per-key limits, burst handling, and what to return over the limit. Several ideas were proposed and rejected along the way, including a Redis token bucket the team vetoed. In the same session she then asked Claude to implement the design. The resulting PR reintroduced the vetoed Redis bucket and missed two edge cases agreed on early in the conversation. The agreed decisions exist only in her notes, not in the repo. What is the most effective next step?
options: Run `/compact keep the agreed rate-limit decisions` and ask the same session to fix the PR according to those decisions.
Have Claude write the agreed decisions to `SPEC.md`, then start a fresh session that builds from that spec as its definition of done.
Add the vetoed approaches to the project CLAUDE.md under a `Never use` heading so every future session avoids them.
Switch the same session to plan mode, ask for a new plan that respects the decisions, and approve it before any editing.
questions.why_correct: El problema es el contexto: la conversación tiene mezcladas las ideas aceptadas con las vetadas. El flujo multi-fase de la doc lo resuelve: lo acordado queda escrito en `SPEC.md` y se construye en una sesión nueva, con contexto limpio y una definición de "hecho" por escrito. Ese mismo archivo después le sirve al reviewer.

why_wrong.0: `/compact` resume la misma conversación, así que puede seguir arrastrando parte del ruido. Y lo acordado no queda en un archivo que se pueda revisar o pasarle al reviewer.
why_wrong.2: `CLAUDE.md` carga en todas las sesiones y es para hechos generales del repo, no para el spec de una feature. Además no resuelve la mezcla de contexto de esta sesión.
why_wrong.3: Mejora la aprobación, pero la sesión sigue teniendo en contexto las tres horas de ideas vetadas, que fueron la causa del error.

questions.rule: Multi-fase: entrevista → `SPEC.md` → sesión nueva que construye → review contra el spec.
questions.source_quote: Once SPEC.md exists, start a fresh session to build from it, so the build begins with a clean context and a written definition of done.

questions.scenario: A payments company on the Enterprise plan turned on Code Review for its GitHub repositories at the Deep review level. Compliance requires that no PR touching `ledger/` merges while a high-severity finding is unresolved and without a person signing off. To automate this, the platform team marked the `Claude Code Review` check run as a required status check in branch protection and removed the human-approval requirement to speed up merges. Two weeks later an auditor finds three merged PRs whose reviews listed high-severity findings in the check run details. Each of those PRs had the check present and completed. Which change satisfies the compliance requirement?
options: Keep the required check and add a `REVIEW.md` on the default branch telling Code Review to fail the check on any high-severity finding.
Comment `@claude review` after every push to `ledger/`, so a fresh review always updates the required check before the merge.
Restore a required human approval in branch protection: Code Review never blocks a PR, and its check run doesn't conclude as a failure.
Replace Code Review with a CI job that runs `/code-review --comment`, and treat a run that posts no comments as approval to merge.
questions.why_correct: Code Review nunca aprueba ni bloquea un PR: la decisión de mergear queda en el equipo. Su check run no concluye como failure, así que marcarlo como requerido no frena nada, solo exige que exista. Para "nadie mergea sin que una persona firme", la última palabra tiene que ser de una persona con branch protection.

why_wrong.0: `REVIEW.md` ajusta qué marca la review, no cambia cómo concluye el check run. La doc no documenta que se pueda hacer fallar el check.
why_wrong.1: Más reviews no cambian que el check nunca falla. Seguiría sin haber nadie que apruebe el merge.
why_wrong.3: Saca a la persona del circuito. La doc avisa que una review sin hallazgos no significa que el código esté libre de errores.

questions.rule: Una review automática informa; la aprobación del merge queda en una persona, con branch protection.
questions.source_quote: A review never approves or blocks the pull request, so the decision to merge stays with your team.

questions.scenario: A team building a webhook retry service follows a multi-phase workflow: a spec session wrote `SPEC.md` with 11 requirements and 6 edge cases, a fresh session implemented it, and that same implementing session was then asked `review your changes and list any problems`. The review returned 23 findings: 19 about naming, comment style, and extra abstraction, and none about the two spec edge cases that were later found untested in staging. The team will keep using Claude for the review step and wants the reviewer to catch spec gaps rather than produce noise. Which review setup is most effective?
options: Have a subagent review the diff against `SPEC.md`, checking each requirement and edge case for tests, and report only correctness gaps, skipping style.
Keep the review in the implementing session but raise the effort to `xhigh` and ask it to list every issue it can find, however small.
Ask the implementing session to re-read `SPEC.md` through an `@SPEC.md` mention and then review its own diff for style and correctness together.
Run `/code-review` in the implementing session with no extra prompt, since its fresh reviewer automatically checks the diff against any spec file.
questions.why_correct: Dos cosas fallaron: el revisor era el mismo que escribió el código, y el pedido no tenía criterio. La doc recomienda un revisor que no haya visto la conversación (un subagente) y, si querés que revise contra el plan en vez de buscar bugs en general, escribir vos el prompt: contra `SPEC.md`, requisito por requisito, con `skip style`.

why_wrong.1: Sigue siendo el autor revisándose, con su razonamiento en contexto. Pedir "todo, por chico que sea" multiplica justo el ruido que querían sacar.
why_wrong.2: Casi: agrega el spec como criterio, pero el revisor sigue siendo el autor, y mezclar estilo con correctitud vuelve a llenar la review de ruido.
why_wrong.3: `/code-review` sí revisa en un subagente fresco, pero busca bugs de correctitud en general: no compara solo contra `SPEC.md`. Para eso la doc dice que escribas el prompt vos.

questions.rule: Review en multi-fase: revisor fresco + criterio explícito (el spec) + `skip style`.
questions.source_quote: If you'd rather have the review check the work against your plan than hunt for bugs in general, write the review prompt yourself:

questions.scenario: A bank wants Claude Code to refactor services in CI but requires a human to approve each plan before any code changes. Its GitHub Actions job runs `claude -p "Plan and then implement the refactor of payments-adapter" --permission-mode plan --allowedTools "Read,Edit,Bash(npm test *)" --output-format json`. Every run ends with exit code 0 and a detailed plan in `result`, but no files ever change, even though `Edit` is in the allowlist. A developer suggests switching to `bypassPermissions` inside the container so the plan gets executed. The approval requirement is audited quarterly, and the team wants an approval trail outside the model. What is the best design?
options: Keep one job but switch to `--permission-mode bypassPermissions`, and add a `Stop` hook that fails the run whenever the tests don't pass.
Keep plan mode and add `--max-turns 40`, since the run stops after planning when it runs out of turns before it can start implementing.
Run one job in `--permission-mode auto` with `don't edit until a human approves the plan` in the prompt, letting the classifier hold edits.
Split it: a plan-mode job posts the plan for review, a protected step records human approval, and a second job implements it with `acceptEdits`.
questions.why_correct: Plan mode mantiene sus bloqueos donde no hay terminal interactiva, incluido `claude -p`: dentro de esa corrida no hay forma de aprobar el plan, por eso nunca edita (aunque `Edit` esté en `--allowedTools`). La aprobación humana tiene que ir ENTRE dos corridas: una planifica, una persona aprueba con registro, y otra implementa con un modo que permita editar.

why_wrong.0: Elimina la aprobación humana, que es el requisito auditado. El `Stop` hook verifica los tests, no aprueba el enfoque.
why_wrong.1: Los turnos no son la causa: en `-p`, plan mode bloquea los edits sin importar cuántos turnos haya.
why_wrong.2: El classifier de auto mode es juicio de un modelo, y una frase en el prompt no deja ningún registro de aprobación. Lo que importa, según la doc, va en reglas o hooks, no en la conversación.

questions.rule: En `-p`, plan mode planifica y nunca edita: la aprobación humana va entre dos corridas.
questions.source_quote: Plan mode keeps its blocks wherever Claude Code runs without an interactive terminal, including non-interactive runs with -p, Agent SDK sessions, and conversations in the VS Code extension's chat panel.

questions.scenario: A team plans every schema change with Claude Code. A developer on Windows is reviewing a seven-step plan Claude proposed for splitting the `orders` table. Halfway through, she realizes the plan assumes the wrong ownership model, and she wants to leave plan mode entirely to discuss the design with a colleague in a normal conversation before any planning resumes. At the approval prompt she presses `Shift+Tab`, the shortcut she always uses to cycle modes, and Claude immediately starts generating migration files. The team now wants its runbook to say how to leave plan mode from the approval prompt without approving anything. What should the runbook say?
options: Choose 'No, keep planning' at the prompt; that option exits plan mode and returns the session to its previous mode without approving.
Press `Esc` first to dismiss the approval prompt, then press `Shift+Tab`; at the prompt itself, `Shift+Tab` approves the plan.
Press `Ctrl+G` to open the plan in the editor, delete its contents and save, which cancels the plan and leaves plan mode.
Type `/plan` again at the approval prompt, which toggles plan mode off and discards the current plan without approving it.
questions.why_correct: La doc lo dice textual: con el prompt de aprobación abierto, apretar `Shift+Tab` aprueba el plan. Por eso Claude empezó a editar. Para salir sin aprobar hay que apretar `Esc` primero y recién después `Shift+Tab`.

why_wrong.0: Casi: "No, keep planning" no aprueba, pero te deja dentro de plan mode para que le digas a Claude qué cambiar. Ella quería salir de plan mode.
why_wrong.2: `Ctrl+G` abre el plan en tu editor para modificarlo antes de que Claude siga. No cancela el plan ni sale de plan mode.
why_wrong.3: `/plan` sirve para entrar a plan mode, no para salir.

questions.rule: En el prompt de aprobación, `Shift+Tab` = aprobar. Para salir sin aprobar: `Esc` y después `Shift+Tab`.
questions.source_quote: At the approval prompt, press Esc first, since pressing Shift+Tab there approves the plan.

questions.scenario: A developer at a SaaS company runs a long Claude Code session in auto mode on Windows, iterating quickly on UI copy and small component fixes. In the middle of that work he needs one risky change: rewriting the session-token refresh in `src/auth/`. He wants Claude to research and propose that change without touching disk, approve the plan himself, and then carry on with the rest of the session as it is, keeping the context he has built up over two hours. His team's `.claude/settings.json` sets no `defaultMode`, and he doesn't want to change anything for teammates or for his future sessions. What is the most effective way to handle the auth change?
options: Send that one prompt as `/plan rewrite the token refresh in src/auth/`, review the plan, and approve it to continue working.
Exit and relaunch with `claude --permission-mode plan`, then paste a summary of the session before asking for the auth plan.
Add `"defaultMode": "plan"` to `.claude/settings.local.json` so it applies only to him, then ask for the auth plan.
Stay in auto mode and write `don't edit src/auth/ until I approve a plan` in the prompt, so the classifier holds those edits.
questions.why_correct: Se entra a plan mode con `Shift+Tab` o con `/plan` delante de un solo prompt, y `/plan <descripción>` además arranca directamente con esa tarea. Al aprobar, la sesión sale de plan mode y pasa al modo de la opción elegida. No reinicia nada ni toca settings: conserva las dos horas de contexto.

why_wrong.1: Funciona, pero pierde el contexto real de la sesión y lo reemplaza por un resumen hecho a mano. Justo lo que quería evitar.
why_wrong.2: `defaultMode` decide cómo ARRANCAN las sesiones nuevas: no cambia la que está corriendo, y dejaría todas sus sesiones futuras de ese repo en plan.
why_wrong.3: El classifier toma frases como esa como señal de bloqueo, pero es un modelo leyendo el transcript, no un bloqueo garantizado, y la frase se puede perder al compactar.

questions.rule: Un prompt riesgoso en medio de una sesión rápida → `/plan <tarea>`. No reinicies ni toques settings.
questions.source_quote: Enter plan mode by pressing Shift+Tab or prefixing a single prompt with /plan.

questions.scenario: A platform team at a retailer is writing guidance for three Claude Code tasks queued this sprint. (1) Rename a misspelled config key in two files of a service that has fast unit tests. (2) Redesign how the checkout service handles partial refunds, touching about 30 files in code few people understand. (3) Replace a deprecated logging call in 180 independent files across the monorepo; each change is mechanical, and the team wants a separate PR per area. Reviewers want human sign-off on the approach wherever the direction is uncertain, but don't want approval ceremonies for trivial edits. Which mapping is most appropriate?
options: (1) plan mode; (2) plan mode followed by `/batch`; (3) a single direct-execution session in `acceptEdits` that edits all 180 files.
(1) direct execution; (2) direct execution with a `Stop` hook running tests; (3) plan mode in one session approving one combined plan.
(1) direct execution; (2) plan mode, with the approach approved before edits; (3) `/batch`, which plans the units and opens PRs after approval.
(1) `/batch`; (2) a `claude -p` loop per file in `dontAsk` mode; (3) plan mode, approving one plan before a single session edits everything.
questions.why_correct: Cada tarea pide una arquitectura distinta. (1) es chica y tiene tests: ejecución directa, sin ceremonia. (2) es compleja y en código poco conocido: plan mode, para aprobar el enfoque antes de editar. (3) es masiva, mecánica e independiente: `/batch` investiga, la descompone en unidades, presenta el plan y, una vez aprobado, lanza un subagente por unidad en su worktree; cada uno abre su PR.

why_wrong.0: Pone ceremonia donde no hace falta (1) y, para (3), un solo diff de 180 archivos sin PR por área.
why_wrong.1: En (2), donde la dirección es incierta, no hay aprobación del enfoque: un `Stop` hook verifica tests, no el diseño. (3) queda en un solo diff combinado.
why_wrong.3: Está al revés: `/batch` para un rename de dos archivos, y la tarea incierta (2) sin ninguna aprobación humana.

questions.rule: Chico y verificable → directo. Complejo o incierto → plan mode. Masivo y mecánico → `/batch`.
questions.source_quote: Researches the codebase, decomposes the work into 5 to 30 independent units, and presents a plan. Once approved, spawns one background subagent per unit in an isolated worktree.
